title: Roman freight: complementary modes and the cost of an entire journey
period: Roman imperial era, with empirical pottery subepisode c. 250–400 CE
summary: An imperial-scale route model and a sharply bounded British pottery study expose why cheaper sea carriage per segment does not determine all door-to-door freight choices.

stages.invention: No single invention investigated; roads, carts, ships and river transport predate the episode.
stages.feasibility: Established land/water transport is documented; ORBIS reconstructs possible routes under stated assumptions.
stages.deployment: Road, river and coastal networks existed; actual lowland British pottery distributions supply the empirical subepisode.
stages.diffusion: No temporal adoption curve. Artifact distributions indicate movement; modeled availability is not measured use.
stages.scaling: Roman-scale connectivity is a reconstructed system property, not an independently identified expansion effect.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Water routes were geographically and seasonally restricted; road and transfer legs remained relevant.
stages.displacement/reversal: No empire-wide displacement or post-Roman collapse is established by this case.

counterevidence: Britain is not the Mediterranean; rural pottery is not army supply or grain. Transport-cost and social-distribution explanations overlap.

episode.technology_configuration: Subepisode A: ORBIS v1 road/river/sea network reconstruction. Subepisode B: distribution of 14 identified late Roman pottery industries in lowland Britain.
episode.task: Move goods between production, distribution and consumption sites; avoid conflating imperial communication speed with freight cost.
episode.population: Modeled travelers and grain shipments in ORBIS; excavated pottery at sampled British settlements in the archaeological study. These are different observational populations.
episode.interval: Model combines Roman-era evidence; pottery evidence c. 250–400 CE.
contemporary_alternatives: local production rather than distant purchase (not directly measured)
episode.adoption_measure: No adopter denominator. Pottery occurrence/proportion by weight and modeled route costs are spatial proxies, not annual transport shares.
episode.observation_limits: Surviving records concentrate on selected places and commodities. Pottery sample is predominantly rural and excludes most military transport; the model treats some nonsynchronous features as contemporaneous.

actors.chooser: Merchants, carriers and officials plausibly made route choices, but their individual choices are not observed here.
actors.payer: Freight purchasers and state redistribution appear in the source framing; actual incidence by class is unknown.
actors.operator_maintainer: Sailors, port workers, carters and road/river maintainers; labour status and repair financing are not measured in this corpus.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Producers, consumers and road/port-adjacent communities; burdens on enslaved or requisitioned workers are not quantified.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown by actor. A reconstructed route does not establish freely chosen use; geography restricted alternatives, but this is not evidence of legal compulsion for a named journey.

labour.tasks: Carriage, loading, unloading, warehousing and transfers are treated as distinct cost-generating tasks; paid/unpaid division unknown.
labour.entry_barriers: Ships, animals and local route knowledge were complements; access to ownership and training not measured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: No direct bargaining or ownership distributions reconstructed.
labour.transition: No individual or cohort labour transition data.
labour.distribution: No group-level income or harm estimates.
labour.evidence_limit: This case tests modal-cost and measurement propositions, not occupational opportunity or living standards.

title: Inka roads and local appropriation in the Atacama
period: c. 1400–1530, with earlier route inheritance and later reuse explicitly distinguished
summary: Inka integration combined inherited roads with logistical facilities, while archaeology in one Atacama district supports local mining exchange beyond a solely state-commanded road economy.

stages.invention: Earlier Andean routes were incorporated; no Inka invention of roads or sole origin is asserted.
stages.feasibility: Roads, drainage, bridges, shelters and stores made travel possible in different environments; local water/forage constraints remained.
stages.deployment: Imperial roads and formal wayside facilities operated alongside local camps and paths.
stages.diffusion: Expansion of connected territory is qualitative; no fraction of subjects using roads is available.
stages.scaling: Imperial incorporation, maintenance and new links expanded a network over c. fifteenth–early sixteenth centuries.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Regular llama caravans are doubtful in the specific dry survey segment; pedestrian movement is inferred, not counted.
stages.displacement/reversal: Regime change did not erase all road use; the 2014 evaluation observes later adaptation and community maintenance, not unchanged operation of the original empire.

counterevidence: Large state-directed mines existed elsewhere. A local absence of state control signatures cannot be generalized to all Inka subjects or all roads.

episode.technology_configuration: An Andean road-and-wayside-supply network; the causal microcase is a 12 km segment beside Cachiyuyo de Llampos mining camps.
episode.task: Official travel/provisioning and possible local craft exchange; these purposes need not have identical users or permissions.
episode.population: Imperial network components in heritage evaluation; camps, roadside sites and travelers inferred from archaeological remains in a 58 km² survey.
episode.interval: Late pre-Hispanic/Inka episode, approximately fifteenth–early sixteenth centuries, with pre-Inka comparisons. Later road survival is a separate observation.
contemporary_alternatives: llama caravans where water and forage permit
highland routes with pasture (not equivalent to the surveyed desert crossing)
episode.adoption_measure: Material distributions and settlement location changes; no census of road users or quantitative diffusion denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Ceramic chronology, surface visibility and selected test excavations; elite narratives and formal architecture disproportionately survive. Local permission and trading volumes are not directly recorded.

actors.chooser: Inka authorities selected integration and supply structures; local artisan-miner households appear to have situated activities near the road.
actors.payer: Imperial and local resources; mit’a and state provisioning are documented in the broader scholarly account, but segment-specific labour budgets are unknown.
actors.operator_maintainer: Road officials, travelers, porters and local communities; exact construction and maintenance allocation at the surveyed segment is unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Subjugated communities and labour contributors; local beneficiaries cannot be treated as representative of all subjects.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Imperial conquest and labour obligations mean subject consent cannot be assumed. Garrido discusses chronicles restricting ordinary road use, but local archaeology suggests limits to control; actual refusal rights at these camps are unknown.

labour.tasks: Road building/maintenance, provisioning, carrying, mining, bead/pigment production and roadside exchange. Paid/unpaid distinction is not safely reducible to modern wages.
labour.entry_barriers: Access to scarce water, ores, paths, supplies and social permissions; specific household exclusion rules unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Official facilities contrast with household production spaces; control of surplus and any tax burden at local camps are not directly observed.
labour.transition: Settlement/craft change between archaeological periods; no tracked individuals or measured retraining duration.
labour.distribution: Some local miners plausibly gained exchange opportunities; no claim that coerced labourers or other communities gained equally.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot quantify net welfare, coercive burden, household income or whether every observed craft expansion was voluntary.

title: Indian railways: trade gains, guarantees and labour under colonial ownership
summary: Distinct studies show trade/income gains, fiscal risk allocation and lower operating costs after state purchases; none is a sufficient statistic for the welfare or consent of all colonial subjects.

stages.invention: Locomotive invention occurred outside this bounded case; the question is deployment of a transferred railway system.
stages.feasibility: Operational lines from 1853; engineering, capital and recurring labour/fuel supply complemented rails.
stages.deployment: Early privately owned companies operated under colonial concession and guarantee arrangements.
stages.diffusion: Network expansion and district connection are measured, not universal household access or use.
stages.scaling: Growth to a large interregional network accompanied expanding trade; timing and ownership differed across companies.
stages.non-adoption/niche: More than 40,000 km of surveyed/planned lines remained unbuilt in Donaldson’s placebo exercise; these are plans, not failed operational services.
stages.displacement/reversal: State purchases changed ownership and incentives; this was institutional reversal within rail, not displacement of rail technology.

counterevidence: Aggregate agricultural gains do not establish worker gains or refute all colonial extraction. Moderate financial returns do not prove absence of extraction through other channels.

episode.technology_configuration: Colonial steam railway network with regulated companies and later state ownership; three linked observational subepisodes retained separately.
episode.task: Transport freight/passengers, connect markets and project state power; finance railway capital and operate services.
episode.population: Donaldson: 192 districts’ agricultural outcomes. Bogart/Chaudhary cost study: railway companies and workers. Investor study: holders of listed securities. No pooling of these outcomes.
episode.interval: Deployment from 1853; district panel 1870–1930; company panel 1874–1912; guaranteed-security return figure 1880–1908.
contemporary_alternatives: public borrowing/ownership versus guaranteed private concessions
episode.adoption_measure: District connected-to-rail indicator, route network, company ownership and operating costs; no population-wide modal share or voluntary adoption denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Colonial records reflect administrative priorities; agricultural output per area is not household income; railway wage/salary data unavailable; secondary-market returns omit many other transfers.

actors.chooser: Colonial Government of India and Secretary of State controlled concessions/placement; company boards made operational choices; users chose shipments under available constraints.
actors.payer: British investors supplied much early capital; Indian tax revenues covered guarantee shortfalls; users paid fares/freight; state purchased companies.
actors.operator_maintainer: Indian and European railway employees; racial segmentation of occupations reported in the cost study.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Taxpayers, railway workers, route-adjacent households and unconnected regions; land losers are not directly sampled here.
actors.ability_to_refuse: No evidence of colonial subjects consenting to guarantees or route plans. Users’ choice among transport modes differs from taxpayers’ exposure; employee exit/refusal and land-acquisition resistance are not directly measured.

labour.tasks: Construction, track maintenance, driving, station operation, handling and administration; ownership change reduced employment relative to comparison paths.
labour.entry_barriers: Study describes Europeans concentrated in more highly paid technical/managerial jobs and Indians in lower-skill work; individual recruitment and training pathways not reconstructed.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Colonial government sought treasury returns and did not depend on workers’ votes; guarantees weakened some private cost incentives.
labour.transition: Company-panel employment change over years around takeovers; no linked displaced-worker cohort or destination-occupation data.
labour.distribution: Operating savings and agricultural gains are observed at different units. Direct wages unavailable; no average person-level gain can be inferred from them.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot determine household net welfare, fiscal opportunity costs, land compensation, individual unemployment duration or overall colonial extraction.

title: Ghana: rail-created commercial geography after railway decline
summary: Railways helped expand cocoa cultivation and towns; later service and maintenance decline coexisted with road replacement and persistent importance of earlier railway places.

stages.invention: Imported railway technology; no invention claim.
stages.feasibility: Western line reached mining areas and Kumasi in 1901–1903.
stages.deployment: Mining and military priorities shaped the western route; eastern construction and wartime delays produced a later connection to Kumasi in 1923.
stages.diffusion: Cocoa and settlement expansion near rail is studied spatially; access and use are not identical.
stages.scaling: Rail transport and commercial agriculture expanded before mid-century.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Several planned routes were not built; their comparison helps test selection rather than showing that rail was technically infeasible.
stages.displacement/reversal: Rail traffic fell after 1974; roads expanded and old rail towns retained importance through 2000.

counterevidence: Later roads preserved absolute transport access; enduring towns do not prove railway operation remained competitive. Cocoa prospects may partly have attracted the eastern line.

episode.technology_configuration: Western and eastern colonial railways, cocoa hinterlands and towns, followed by post-independence road expansion and rail decline.
episode.task: Move heavy mining inputs and exports, troops, cocoa and people; later sustain transport as rail service deteriorated.
episode.population: Historical grid cells, cocoa-producing areas and towns in the study, not a panel of individual farmers or workers.
episode.interval: Construction from 1898; early comparisons 1901–1931; persistence to 2000.
episode.adoption_measure: Rail proximity, cocoa production, census settlement size and later economic proxies; reported modal cocoa shares are contextual historical series. No generic national technology-adoption rate.
episode.observation_limits: Main identification uses selected forest-zone cells and excludes major endpoint cities in relevant specifications; historical sources and transport substitutes vary over time.

actors.chooser: Colonial governors, mining interests and railway planners initially; African farmers responded to opportunities; post-independence authorities managed rail/road investment.
actors.payer: Colonial/public finance, railway users and producers; precise incidence and labour financing not independently reconstructed here.
actors.operator_maintainer: Railway staff, construction/repair labour, carriers, road operators and cocoa cultivators; employment totals appear in historical narrative but individual careers do not.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Railway workers, bypassed places, forest users and households dependent on local land; precise dispossession and compulsory labour incidence unknown.
actors.ability_to_refuse: The rail network served colonial military power, but that does not establish every producer’s participation was coerced. Farmer use, worker contracts, taxation and community land consent require separate evidence not available here.

labour.tasks: Rail construction/maintenance, port and station handling, farming, head-loading and later road transport; the study identifies reorganization without a complete occupation balance.
labour.entry_barriers: Land and crop maturation, market access and equipment matter; tenure, migrant status and capital access are not measured consistently.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Colonial route priorities differed from farmer interests; later management and fiscal weakness affected service. Local bargaining institutions are not independently examined.
labour.transition: Long-run settlement/census sequence and aggregate rail employment context; no individual labour-cohort tracking.
labour.distribution: Connected places grew, but no inference that all farmers, landholders or railway workers benefited equally. Forest conversion is described, not monetized.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot equate urban persistence with optimal location, general welfare or absence of coercion/externalities.

title: Early electric vehicles: a service system fails, specialized uses persist
period: 1897–1925, distinguishing EVC 1897–1907 from later utility/fleet efforts
summary: Early electric mobility offered a managed cab-service configuration and later fleet niches; EVC failure and the wider private-car outcome require different explanations.

stages.invention: No first inventor claimed; propulsion and accumulator development precede this episode.
stages.feasibility: Electric cabs operated in New York in 1897; repeatable service did not establish profitability.
stages.deployment: Fleet ownership retained maintenance and operational control within a service enterprise.
stages.diffusion: Expansion to multiple cities is documented qualitatively, but no consistent adopter denominator is supplied.
stages.scaling: EVC attempted system expansion and suffered business failures; later utilities coordinated EV promotion from 1909.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Task-specific fleets persisted in the comparative literature, including commercial delivery and special services; not equivalent to winning the general private-car market.
stages.displacement/reversal: Regional EVC ventures failed around 1901–1902; parent default in 1907. Private gasoline cars expanded while electric applications survived selectively.

counterevidence: General gasoline advantages were real. Neither an electric niche nor a counterfactual earlier EV association establishes that electric cars could profitably dominate all travel.

episode.technology_configuration: A: New York and affiliated EVC electric-cab service with retained ownership. B: utility-supported US fleet/charging efforts 1909–1925. C: general private-car displacement with European specialty fleets used only as bounded negative comparisons.
episode.task: Sell reliable local passenger trips or perform predictable fleet work; private touring is a different task.
episode.population: Operating companies, utilities and selected fleet applications in historical scholarship. No common statistical population across subepisodes.
episode.interval: 1897–1925; EVC operational and parent-company failures explicitly separated.
contemporary_alternatives: electric fleet operation versus privately maintained electric cars
episode.adoption_measure: Documented operation, expansion/failure dates and associations’ activities; no harmonized market-share series used.
episode.observation_limits: Kirsch article summarizes a dissertation; early cost reports self-reported and retrospectively evaluated. Mom compares tasks and regions; this contribution does not reconstruct his entire archival base.

actors.chooser: Entrepreneurs chose service versus sales models; utilities chose promotional support; fleet managers and wealthy early private buyers chose equipment.
actors.payer: Company investors and fares, vehicle buyers and participating utilities; distribution of financial losses not fully reconstructed.
actors.operator_maintainer: Specialist fleet workers, drivers, battery attendants and private owners; maintaining lead-acid batteries could not be omitted.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Employees of failed firms, pedestrians and urban residents exposed to competing transport systems; health burdens not quantified.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Buyer choice among vehicle types does not measure worker bargaining or residents’ ability to refuse street hazards. Precise contract and exit conditions are unknown.

labour.tasks: Driving, vehicle/battery maintenance, charging, dispatch and utility coordination; service ownership kept some tasks with specialists.
labour.entry_barriers: Capital, technical maintenance and access to charging; gender/status imagery discussed in scholarship but not used here as quantified causal evidence.
labour.bargaining_ownership: EVC retained vehicle assets; dispersed private buyers bore more operational responsibility. Worker bargaining contracts not inspected.
labour.transition: Company survival dates and technology/task comparisons; no evidence of which workers moved into gasoline vehicle employment or how long adjustment took.
labour.distribution: Some fleet tasks remained viable; no total employment or household-welfare estimate.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer profitable universal electrification, worker gains, or spontaneous consumer preferences solely from the dominant technology.

title: Containerization: interoperable equipment, trade and contested dock work
period: 1956–1990; US labour negotiations 1960–1987 explicitly separated from global trade outcomes
summary: Compatible equipment and institutional settlements expanded container systems, while published trade estimates and labour records sharply limit simple claims of universally shared efficiency gains.

stages.invention: Boxes and earlier experiments predated the postwar system; no single-inventor claim.
stages.feasibility: 1956 Ideal-X commercial US voyage demonstrates one operational configuration, not global scalability.
stages.deployment: Shipping lines and terminals invested in cranes, ships and facilities; US and ISO standardization followed distinct negotiations.
stages.diffusion: Published study dates country-level first port/rail facilities during 1966–1983 and follows trade through 1990; first facility is not saturation.
stages.scaling: Intermodal compatibility, equipment, leasing and state/military demand supported expansion; many products/locations had different utilization.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Prewar attempts and early port reluctance are documented; some products remained unsuited to containers and break-bulk/bulk alternatives coexisted.
stages.displacement/reversal: Many manual dock tasks were removed or relocated; new handling and off-dock work were contested rather than equivalent for all workers.

counterevidence: Large adoption-date trade estimates fail some pre-trend tests. Negotiated compensation does not prove complete compensation; technological substitution also shifts work between groups.

episode.technology_configuration: A: international standardized container port/rail system in the trade panel. B: US West Coast labour agreements and off-dock work jurisdiction. These populations are kept distinct.
episode.task: Transfer freight across modes with less repeated cargo handling; preserve or reallocate work and finance technological adjustment.
episode.population: 157-country bilateral product-trade sample in published econometrics; specific PMA/ILWU/Teamster employers and workers in US court records.
episode.interval: US deployment 1956; global adoption measure 1966–1983/trade through 1990; West Coast agreements and dispute 1960–1987.
contemporary_alternatives: bulk or roll-on/roll-off systems for unsuitable products
company-specific container sizes and handling systems
episode.adoption_measure: First port or rail container facilities by country; product-containerizability interactions; separately, documented work rules and litigated task jurisdiction. No worker-consent or worldwide welfare measure.
episode.observation_limits: Containerizability changes over time; country adoption is coarse; trade-policy and selection confounding persist; court disputes do not represent all labour markets.

actors.chooser: Shipping firms, port authorities, standards bodies and state/military purchasers chose investments and specifications; union/employer negotiators chose some work-rule terms.
actors.payer: Private capital, public subsidies/port investments, freight users and employer-financed compensation; assessment incidence was litigated.
actors.operator_maintainer: Crane operators, longshore workers, drivers, off-dock freight-station workers and equipment maintainers; no full staffing balance reconstructed.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers outside protected bargaining groups, bypassed ports and nearby communities; global producer and resident impacts are not fully observed.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Union bargaining could condition work-rule changes, but negotiations do not imply universal consent. Teamsters and nonmember operators contested claimed jurisdiction; bypassed ports and residents had different, unmeasured voice.

labour.tasks: Less repeated break-bulk handling; mechanized lifting; stuffing/unstuffing relocated partly off-dock; changed maintenance and dispatch requirements.
labour.entry_barriers: Capital and compatible equipment; union jurisdiction and employer-association membership structured access to work. Individual training barriers not quantified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: PMA/ILWU fund and work-rule bargain; later disputes show competing longshore and Teamster claims. Investors, workers and shippers had separate interests.
labour.transition: 1960 agreement, subsequent unanticipated work losses and litigation through 1987 show a prolonged institutional transition; no complete person-level cohort.
labour.distribution: A $29m fund is documented and funding charges differed by shipper; it is not evidence that all job or community losses were covered.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer net employment, complete compensation, global wage effects, land displacement or pollution costs from trade growth.

title: Singapore container terminals: state planning and scarce waterfront land
period: 1972–2000, with the 2000 official account retrospectively describing earlier choices
summary: Singapore’s official terminal-opening account makes port expansion an organizational and land-allocation project as well as a handling technology; its celebratory perspective limits causal and distributional conclusions.

stages.invention: Container technology already operated elsewhere; Singapore’s case is adoption and adaptation.
stages.feasibility: Container berths operated from 1972 according to the official account.
stages.deployment: Tanjong Pagar berths were commissioned and conventional berths progressively converted.
stages.diffusion: No adoption denominator; the account describes growing terminal use and shipping-line conversion.
stages.scaling: Pasir Panjang planning and construction culminated in a 2000 opening, with workforce and information-service complements.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Alternative waterfront uses competed with port development; no systematic sample of rejected port options inspected.
stages.displacement/reversal: Waterfront use changed; resident relocation, losses and compensation are not measured in the speech.

counterevidence: The primary source is the government’s success narrative. It cannot establish that stated planning choices were uniquely necessary or that affected communities benefited.

episode.technology_configuration: Tanjong Pagar container berths from 1972 and Pasir Panjang expansion opened in 2000.
episode.task: Accommodate container shipping and port services within scarce urban waterfront space.
episode.population: Government/port authority as adopter and official narrator; shipping lines and workforce discussed, residents not sampled.
episode.interval: 1972–2000; exact decision-date controversies before 1972 are not resolved here.
contemporary_alternatives: other port locations or staged expansion (not comparatively costed in the inspected source)
episode.adoption_measure: Commissioning and expansion chronology in a government speech; no consistent throughput denominator used.
episode.observation_limits: Retrospective political self-presentation; claimed productivity and future designs are not independently audited in this case.

actors.chooser: Singapore government and Port of Singapore Authority, according to the speech.
actors.payer: Port/state investment is implied; exact financing and ultimate cost incidence are not stated adequately in the inspected paragraphs.
actors.operator_maintainer: Terminal workforce and operators of equipment/information services; maintenance financing and unpaid work are unmeasured.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Users of competing waterfront space, adjacent residents and workers facing task change; their accounts are absent.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown for residents and individual workers. State selection of port land does not establish popular consent or an effective option to refuse displacement.

labour.tasks: Shift from manual cargo handling toward crane operations, information management and related services described by government.
labour.entry_barriers: Workforce upgrading claimed; actual training access, credential requirements and exclusion unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: State/port authority control is visible; union and worker bargaining evidence absent.
labour.transition: Long planning horizon documented, but no worker-cohort transition measured.
labour.distribution: No disaggregated incomes, displacement compensation or health outcomes.
labour.evidence_limit: An operationally successful port and official pride do not establish net benefits for every land user or worker.
